title: The Idiot Who Talked About Discovery Learning at Interview
author: Chris Reid
source: The Curiosity Gap (chris-reid.co.uk, via Substack), June 8, 2026, 6.12.26
summary: Reid opens with a personal story -- losing a job offer at a Michaela-style school after describing a lesson that sounded too much like 'discovery learning' -- as a way into a broader argument about how the influential Kirschner, Sweller and Clark (2006) paper has been used in English education policy. He agrees the paper was a genuine corrective against pure, unguided discovery learning, but argues its legacy has curdled into something he calls 'total instruction': a system that strips out teacher judgement entirely rather than simply favoring more guidance. Working through the evidence -- Mayer's older synthesis, a 2011 meta-analysis of 164 studies, and the EEF's underpowered project-based-learning RCT -- he concludes the honest research verdict is that pure discovery doesn't work (a claim nobody actually defends anymore), that robustly comparing direct instruction to moderately guided instruction is very hard given how much teacher judgement both require, and that the real live question is not which single method wins but how much latitude teachers should be given to choose. His central analogy compares this to parenting: nobody demands that all parents use one instructional method across every situation, from teaching traffic safety to letting a child use a climbing frame, because good parents calibrate to the child and the stakes. He closes arguing that the current risk to education isn't direct instruction winning the argument -- it's the systematic deskilling of teachers by removing their judgement altogether, at the exact moment the DfE is piloting AI tutoring.
points: Reid's core distinction is between defensible 'direct/explicit instruction' and what he calls 'total instruction' -- a lethal mutation (borrowing Haertel's term via Haili Hughes) that strips out the teacher judgement, discussion, and calibrated risk-taking that good direct instruction actually depends on.

He cites a 2011 meta-analysis of 164 studies showing explicit instruction beats unassisted discovery by roughly 5 months' progress, but that 'assisted/enhanced discovery' -- a form of moderately guided instruction -- beat other approaches (including some forms of explicit instruction) by 4 months, undercutting a simple 'direct instruction always wins' reading of the evidence.

His parenting analogy reframes the entire debate: nobody asks which single method the best parents use across every situation, because good parenting (and, he argues, good teaching) calibrates guidance to the child, the task, and the stakes rather than applying one method universally.

He argues the deeper danger is a 'vicious cycle': if teachers are never trained to exercise judgement about how much guidance to give, of course they do it badly -- which then gets used as further justification for stripping out judgement altogether.
quotes: The phone call I got later that evening wasn’t a surprise: ‘we don’t do discovery learning here,’ he told me.

This is not the fault of KSC and it is not what they argue for, but I see it as a sign that their argument has been twisted to suit a particular position: teachers have knowledge and must pass this on didactically by talking; teacher judgement should be removed and students are passive recipients of information.

First, 'pure discovery learning' doesn't work. But then, nobody is defending pure discovery learning... What we should be debating is how much guidance enquiry needs -- not whether to abandon all guidance.
Nobody is asking which instructional methods the most effective parents are using at home so that we can get less effective parents to follow their lead.
Total instruction has no defenders -- only a system that finds teacher judgement inconvenient.
Of all the times in the history of education, this is the most dangerous to be systematically deskilling teachers.
